sentences.text: Ada noticed it because of the wires.
There were four wires across the yard behind the flats, and everything sat on them.
Pigeons sat on them in a row like a badly made fence.
Starlings sat on them and shouted.
A collared dove sat on the middle one every afternoon in the same spot and did nothing whatsoever for an hour at a time, which Ada respected.
The swifts never sat on them.

They came in May and they were gone in August and for those three months they went over the yard at eleven o'clock at night still screaming, in loops, four and five together, at a speed that made the pigeons look like furniture.
And in all of it — she watched properly, from the fire escape, for two summers — not one of them ever landed on anything.
Not the aerial, not the flat roof of the bin store, not the one tree.
She mentioned it to her mother, who said they must land somewhere, everything lands somewhere.
She mentioned it to her teacher, who said it was a good observation and moved on.
She mentioned it to Mr Iqbal on the ground floor, who had been a merchant seaman and now had a telescope pointed permanently at nothing in particular, and Mr Iqbal put down his tea and said, "Ah.
Now you've asked the right person the right question, which almost never happens, so I'm going to enjoy this."
